text: A Helm chart is a package of pre-configured Kubernetes resource templates, bundled with a default values file and metadata declared in Chart.yaml.
Helm templates are written in the Go template language and are rendered into concrete Kubernetes manifests at install time.
Helm injects configuration into templates through the .Values object, whose contents come from values.yaml.
Values in a Helm chart can be overridden at install time with --set flags or by passing additional files with -f/--values.
Running 'helm install' renders a chart's templates with the merged values and applies the resulting manifests to the Kubernetes cluster.
A Helm release is a specific instance of a chart deployed to a cluster, tracked by a unique release name.
Helm chart dependencies are declared in Chart.yaml and fetched into the charts/ subdirectory before rendering.
In Helm 2, releases were managed by a cluster-side server component called Tiller, which held broad permissions.
Helm 3 removed Tiller entirely; it runs fully client-side and stores release state as Secrets in the target namespace.
A values.yaml file is optional in a Helm chart; a chart whose templates define no required values can install without one.
A Kubernetes Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, which in turn keeps a desired number of identical Pods running.
A Deployment enables declarative rollouts and rollbacks by creating and updating the ReplicaSet it owns.
If the replicas field is not set, a Kubernetes Deployment defaults to a single replica.
A Kubernetes Service provides a stable network endpoint and load-balances traffic across the Pods selected by its label selector.
A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs that Pods can consume as environment variables or mounted files.
A Secret holds sensitive data such as passwords or tokens; by default it is only base64-encoded, not encrypted, at rest.
A namespace partitions cluster resources, scoping names and providing a boundary for quotas and access control.
A Pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes and can hold one or more tightly coupled containers sharing a network namespace.
Kustomize is an alternative to Helm that patches raw Kubernetes manifests with overlays instead of using a templating language.
The platform base chart overrides the Kubernetes default and sets replicas to 3 for every service unless a team opts out.
On this platform, Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted at rest using a KMS provider configured on the API server, rather than left as plain base64.
Terraform state maps real-world infrastructure to the resources declared in configuration and stores metadata Terraform uses to plan changes.
Terraform state can be stored locally in a terraform.tfstate file or in a remote backend such as an S3 bucket.
A remote Terraform backend enables state locking so that concurrent runs do not corrupt shared state.
Terraform configuration is written in HCL across .tf files that declare providers, resources, and variables.
terraform plan previews the changes Terraform will make, while terraform apply executes them and updates the state.
Terraform input variables are declared with variable blocks and can be set via tfvars files, -var flags, or environment variables.
Unlike Helm, Terraform does not use a values.yaml file; its configuration lives in .tf files and its runtime inputs in variables.
GitOps tools such as Argo CD can deploy Helm charts by rendering them and continuously syncing the output to a cluster.
A Docker image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile, and a container is a running instance of that image.
Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new image layer, and layers are cached to speed up subsequent builds.
A container registry such as Docker Hub or ECR stores and distributes built images by repository and tag.
Multi-stage Docker builds use several FROM stages so the final image contains only runtime artifacts, not build tooling.
The ENTRYPOINT instruction sets the executable a container runs, while CMD provides default arguments to it.
Docker volumes persist data outside a container's writable layer so it survives container restarts and removals.
Docker Compose defines multi-container applications in a compose file, wiring services, networks, and volumes together.
Bind mounts map a host directory into a container, which is useful for local development but ties the container to the host layout.
An image tag labels a specific build of a repository; 'latest' is just a conventional tag, not a guarantee of the newest image.
The Docker daemon builds, runs, and manages containers, while the docker CLI talks to it over a socket or TCP.
A .dockerignore file excludes paths from the build context so large or sensitive files are not sent to the daemon.
Containers on the same Docker network can reach each other by service name through Docker's embedded DNS.
A CI/CD pipeline is a sequence of automated stages that build, test, and deploy code on each change.
GitHub Actions workflows are defined in YAML under .github/workflows and are triggered by repository events such as push or pull_request.
A workflow job runs on a runner, and steps within a job execute sequentially in the same environment.
Build artifacts produced in one CI job can be uploaded and downloaded by later jobs in the same pipeline.
Caching dependencies between CI runs avoids re-downloading packages and speeds up builds.
A matrix build runs the same job across combinations of parameters, such as multiple language versions.
CI secrets are stored encrypted and injected into jobs as environment variables, never committed to the repository.
A merge gate blocks a pull request from merging until required checks, such as tests, pass.
Jenkins pipelines are defined in a Jenkinsfile and executed by agents connected to the Jenkins controller.
A deployment stage promotes a built artifact to an environment such as staging or production, often with manual approval.
Blue-green deployment runs two production environments and switches traffic to the new one once it is verified.
A canary release routes a small fraction of traffic to a new version before rolling it out fully.
Prometheus collects metrics by scraping HTTP endpoints that expose time-series data at a fixed interval.
A Prometheus counter only increases, while a gauge can go up and down to represent a current value.
A histogram metric buckets observations so percentiles like p95 latency can be computed.
Grafana queries data sources such as Prometheus and renders dashboards of panels and charts.
Alerting rules fire when a query crosses a threshold for a sustained duration, notifying an alertmanager.
Observability is often described through three signals: metrics, logs, and traces.
OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral APIs and SDKs for emitting traces, metrics, and logs.
A distributed trace follows a request across services using a shared trace ID and per-operation spans.
An SLO sets a target for a service-level indicator, and the error budget is the allowed shortfall from it.
PromQL is the query language used to select and aggregate Prometheus time series.
Exporters translate third-party system metrics into the Prometheus exposition format.
Log aggregation ships logs from many sources into a central store for search and correlation.
DNS resolves human-readable hostnames into IP addresses that clients connect to.
A load balancer distributes incoming connections across multiple backend servers to share load.
A Kubernetes Ingress exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to Services inside it.
TLS encrypts traffic in transit and authenticates the server using a certificate signed by a trusted authority.
A firewall allows or blocks traffic based on rules over source, destination, port, and protocol.
CIDR notation expresses an IP range as an address and a prefix length, such as 10.0.0.0/16.
A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them, often adding TLS or caching.
A service mesh adds a sidecar proxy to each service to handle traffic routing, retries, and mTLS.
HTTP status codes in the 2xx range indicate success, 4xx client errors, and 5xx server errors.
A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy restricts which Pods can communicate with each other at the network layer.
Amazon EC2 provides resizable virtual machine instances in the cloud.
Amazon S3 is an object storage service that stores files as objects in buckets.
AWS IAM manages users, roles, and policies that control access to AWS resources.
A VPC is an isolated virtual network in AWS where you launch resources into subnets.
AWS Lambda runs code in response to events without provisioning servers.
Amazon EKS is a managed Kubernetes control plane that runs the Kubernetes API for you.
Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service handling backups, patching, and failover.
Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms for AWS resources and applications.
An auto-scaling group adjusts the number of EC2 instances based on demand or a schedule.
AWS regions contain multiple availability zones, which are isolated data-center groups.
A security group acts as a stateful virtual firewall controlling inbound and outbound traffic to an instance.
An Elastic Load Balancer spreads traffic across targets in multiple availability zones.
A Git commit records a snapshot of the staged changes along with a message and parent reference.
A branch in Git is a movable pointer to a commit, used to develop features in isolation.
Merging combines the histories of two branches, creating a merge commit when they have diverged.
Rebasing replays commits from one branch onto another to produce a linear history.
A remote is a named reference to another copy of the repository, such as origin on a hosting service.
A pull request proposes merging one branch into another and is the unit of code review on hosting platforms.
A Git tag marks a specific commit, commonly used to label releases.
git stash temporarily shelves uncommitted changes so the working directory is clean.
git cherry-pick applies the changes from a specific commit onto the current branch.
The reflog records where HEAD and branch tips have pointed, allowing recovery of lost commits.
In Linux, each running program is a process identified by a PID and owned by a user.
File permissions in Linux are expressed as read, write, and execute bits for owner, group, and others.
systemd manages services as units and controls their startup, dependencies, and logging.
cron schedules commands to run at fixed times or intervals via crontab entries.
A pipe connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next.
grep searches text for lines matching a pattern, and sed and awk transform streams of text.
Environment variables pass configuration to processes and are inherited by child processes.
A signal such as SIGTERM asks a process to terminate, while SIGKILL forces it to stop.
Package managers like apt and yum install, update, and remove software from configured repositories.
Standard streams are stdin, stdout, and stderr, referenced by file descriptors 0, 1, and 2.
Relational databases store data in tables with fixed schemas and relate rows with keys.
NoSQL databases trade rigid schemas for flexible document, key-value, or wide-column models.
An index speeds up lookups on a column at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.
A transaction groups operations so they all commit or all roll back, following ACID properties.
A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column between them.
Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy, while denormalization trades it for read speed.
Replication copies data to replicas for availability and read scaling, often with a primary for writes.
Sharding partitions data across multiple database nodes to scale beyond one machine.
A connection pool reuses database connections to avoid the cost of opening one per request.
A schema migration applies versioned changes to a database's structure in a controlled order.
Role-based access control grants permissions to roles, and users inherit permissions from their roles.
OAuth 2.0 lets an application obtain delegated access to a resource on behalf of a user without sharing passwords.
A JWT is a signed token carrying claims that a server can verify without a database lookup.
The principle of least privilege grants each identity only the permissions it needs.
A secrets manager stores and rotates credentials, issuing them to applications at runtime.
Encryption in transit protects data on the network, while encryption at rest protects stored data.
Vulnerability scanning inspects images and dependencies for known security issues.
A Kubernetes RBAC Role grants permissions on resources within a namespace, bound to subjects by a RoleBinding.
Mutual TLS authenticates both the client and the server using certificates.
Audit logs record who did what and when, supporting investigation and compliance.
A DaemonSet runs a copy of a Pod on every node, commonly used for log and metrics agents.
A StatefulSet manages Pods with stable network identities and persistent storage for stateful apps.
A Job runs Pods to completion for batch work, and a CronJob runs Jobs on a schedule.
A HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales the number of Pods based on observed metrics such as CPU.
A PersistentVolumeClaim requests storage, which is satisfied by a PersistentVolume in the cluster.
A node is a worker machine in Kubernetes that runs Pods and is managed by the control plane.
Taints on a node repel Pods unless the Pods have a matching toleration.
Labels are key-value pairs attached to objects, and selectors match objects by their labels.
An init container runs to completion before the main containers in a Pod start.
A liveness probe restarts an unhealthy container, while a readiness probe gates traffic to it.
Resource requests reserve CPU and memory for a Pod, and limits cap how much it can use.
The kube-scheduler assigns Pods to nodes based on resource availability and constraints.
A Python virtual environment isolates a project's dependencies from the system interpreter.
pip installs Python packages from an index such as PyPI into the active environment.
pytest discovers and runs test functions and reports assertions that fail.
Type hints annotate expected types and are checked by tools like mypy, not at runtime.
async and await let Python run I/O-bound coroutines concurrently on an event loop.
A decorator wraps a function to extend its behavior without modifying its body.
The logging module emits records at levels such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, and ERROR.
A requirements file or pyproject.toml pins a project's dependencies for reproducible installs.
Apache Kafka is a distributed log that stores streams of records in partitioned, ordered topics.
A message queue decouples producers from consumers by buffering messages until they are processed.
In publish-subscribe, publishers send messages to a topic and all subscribers receive a copy.
A Kafka consumer group splits partitions among its members so each record is processed once per group.
Event-driven architectures react to events asynchronously rather than through direct calls.
